en: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system, with a diameter of about 140,000 kilometers, making it roughly 11 times wider than Earth.
The Moon orbits Earth at an average distance of 384,400 kilometers, meaning light takes about 1.3 seconds to bounce off it and reach us.
Our Sun is a medium-sized star that is so massive you could fit about 1.3 million Earths inside its total volume.
About 97 percent of all water on Earth is found in the salty oceans, leaving only three percent as fresh water for drinking.
On the Mohs hardness scale, talc is the softest mineral at level one, while diamond is the hardest natural mineral at level ten.
The highest officially recorded air temperature on Earth was 56.7 degrees Celsius, measured in Death Valley, California, in the year 1913.
The strongest earthquake ever recorded was the 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile, which reached a massive magnitude of 9.5.
It can take up to 500 years for nature to form just one single inch of fertile topsoil from weathered rock and decaying plants.
The troposphere, the lowest layer of Earth's atmosphere where all our weather happens, extends about 12 kilometers above the Earth's surface.
Because Neptune is so far from the Sun, it takes the ice giant a full 165 Earth years to complete just one single orbit.
Measured from its underwater base to its snowy peak, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is Earth's tallest mountain at over 10,200 meters high.
The Moon is much smaller than Earth, with a diameter of 3,474 kilometers, which is roughly one-quarter the width of our planet.
